fetched_contents.text: Family meals are associated with lower substance use in female adolescents Abstract Adolescents, especially female youth, who have more family meals tend to be at lower risk for substance use. The present study tested whether family meals relate to substance use count and frequency during high school, whether associations differ by gender, and whether other family‐related variables explain these associations. A community sample of 316 adolescents (M age = 16.40, SD = 0.74; 56.96% female; 41.77% Latine, 23.10% Asian American, 29.11% European American, 6.01% from other ethnic backgrounds including Middle Eastern and African American) reported the number of substances they have ever used and how often they used alcohol, marijuana, and cigarettes, and completed measures of parental support and family cohesion. Across 15 days, they reported whether they had a family meal, got along with parents, and spent leisure time with their family each day. Regression models tested associations between frequency of family meals and substance use, whether associations differed by gender, and whether associations were explained by other family‐related variables. Results indicated that more frequent family meals were associated with lower substance use count and less frequent alcohol, marijuana, and cigarette use among female adolescents but not male adolescents. Other daily family experiences were unrelated to substance use, and family meal frequency was independently related to lower substance use after accounting for parental support and family cohesion. Taken together, more frequent family meals in high school may reduce substance use risk for female adolescents, and interventions could consider promoting family meals in addition to other positive family values. Keywords: adolescent, family dinner, family meals, substance use ---------------------------------------- During adolescence, youth are at heightened risk of substance use initiation and escalation (Johnston et al., 2023). More frequent substance use in adolescence typically leads to greater substance abuse and dependence in adulthood (Grant & Dawson, 1997). Family Systems Theory and developmental risk models posit that family relationships and experiences including family rituals impact youth's behaviors and adjustment (Kerr & Bowen, 1988). Frequent family meals—or having a meal with another family member, including a sibling or caregiver—can be a stable routine that promotes family relationships and communication, with evidence suggesting stronger associations in female relative to male youth (Eisenberg et al., 2008; Fisher et al., 2007; White & Halliwell, 2011). However, few studies have tested whether adolescents who have frequent family meals may have lower substance use risk and whether other family activities and aspects of relationships (e.g., family cohesion and leisure time) may explain this association. In the present study, we examined whether family meals were related to adolescents' substance use count and frequency of alcohol, marijuana, and cigarette use, whether associations differed by gender, and whether associations were explained by other family activities and relationships. Family meals are related to better adolescent well‐being and healthier dietary habits (Hammons & Fiese, 2011; Utter et al., 2017), but associations between family meals and substance use risk are relatively less consistent (Goldfarb et al., 2015). More frequent family meals have been related to lower risk for substance use, including lower frequency of alcohol, marijuana, and tobacco use both concurrently and years later (Eisenberg et al., 2004, 2008; Fulkerson et al., 2009; Levin et al., 2012; Sen, 2010), with stronger associations in female than in male adolescents (Eisenberg et al., 2008; Fisher et al., 2007; White & Halliwell, 2011). Family meals can serve as a family ritual, imparting stability within the home (Skeer et al., 2018). Youth who engage in these family rituals and routines tend to feel connected to their families, which may deter them from engaging in risky behaviors outside the home such as engagement with deviant peers or substance use (Brown et al., 2019; Fiese et al., 2002; Fulkerson et al., 2006). Routines such as family meals also have symbolic significance by fostering a shared family identity (Fiese, 1992; Wolin & Bennett, 1984). Attending family rituals including a regular dinnertime has been found to reduce at‐risk children's likelihood of alcoholism, and the disruption of such rituals is thought to contribute to the intergenerational transmission of alcoholism from parents to youth (Bennett et al., 1987; Wolin et al., 1980). Satisfaction with family rituals has been related to greater self‐reliance and other aspects of psychosocial development in late adolescence (Eaker & Walters, 2002). These experiences may be particularly impactful for female adolescents because girls tend to be more affiliative than boys during adolescence (Cyranowski et al., 2000; Feingold, 1994). Evidence suggests that family interactions and relationships are more related to female adolescents' mental health and substance use compared to that of male adolescents (Dakof, 2000; Davies & Lindsay, 2004; Keijsers et al., 2010; Skeer et al., 2011; Telzer & Fuligni, 2013). For example, female adolescents tend to be more emotionally affected by interpersonal conflict (Chung et al., 2009; Flook, 2012) and physiologically linked with their parents during family conflict relative to male adolescents (Saxbe et al., 2014), both of which can contribute to psychopathology and risk‐taking behavior (e.g., Piehler & Dishion, 2014; Rahal, Alkon, et al., 2023; Rahal, Shirtcliff, et al., 2023). Family meals also provide time for families to discuss daily events (Hammons & Fiese, 2011; Skeer et al., 2018). fetched_contents.text: Does TV viewing during family meals make a difference in adolescent substance use? Abstract Objective Family meals are important to adolescent health, but relatively little is known about TV viewing during family meals. The present paper examines the role that TV viewing during family meals may have on substance use behaviors among adolescents. Methods A diverse sample of 806 Minnesota high school students (mean age 17.2 years) provided survey data in 2003–2004 regarding family meal frequency, substance use behavior and general family connectedness. General linear modeling was used to compare substance use across three family meal/TV categories in a cross-sectional analysis. Results 28.6% of participants ate regular family meals without TV, and 27.5% had regular family meals while watching TV. Significant differences in cigarette smoking, alcohol and marijuana use were found for females reporting regular family meals versus no regular family meals, but did not differ significantly by TV viewing. No significant differences were found across groups of males. Conclusions Results from this study indicate that TV viewing during family meals does not appear to attenuate the previously observed protective relationship between family meals and substance use for females. Benefits of family meals may be derived simply from having adolescents at home during mealtimes. Keywords Adolescents ; Family meals ; Substance use Introduction A growing body of research suggests that the frequency of family meals is important to adolescent health. Given the high prevalence of substance use in adolescents, it is of great interest that studies have found that regular family meals are associated with lower risk for cigarette smoking, alcohol and marijuana use in adolescents, particularly among girls (Eisenberg et al., 2004, National Center on Addiction and Substance Use, 2007, Eisenberg et al., 2008). Because general family functioning, or “connectedness,” has been associated with substance use behaviors (Resnick et al., 1997) and family meals, it is important to consider the role of meals above and beyond this broader family characteristic. Although most studies on family meals have focused on their frequency, a few studies have begun to examine the context or characteristics of family meals, such as structure, location, and television viewing (Fitzpatrick et al., 2007, Fulkerson et al., 2008, Boutelle et al., 2003, Feldman et al., 2007, Neumark-Sztainer et al., 2008). Existing research on TV viewing during family meals has focused largely on dietary intake and eating behaviors, and has identified some differences in outcomes related to TV viewing during meals. To our knowledge, the role of TV viewing during family meals has not been investigated vis-à-vis substance use. More detailed information on contextual characteristics of family meals has the potential to guide the public health and medical community in making evidence-based recommendations to parents. Research regarding TV viewing during family meals can also reveal mechanisms underlying the observed association between regular family meals and substance use behaviors among adolescents. Thus, the aim of this paper is to examine the role TV viewing during family meals may have on substance abuse behaviors among adolescents. fetched_contents.text: Gender differences in family meal frequency and their association with substance use and mental health among middle and high school students Background: Family meals are associated with adolescent health outcomes. Studies have reported that girls are less likely than boys to have dinner with their families. Purpose: This study examined gender differences in family meal frequency and the relationship between meal frequency and other health measures, using a large and representative sample of California middle and high school students. Methods: This study analyzed data from the 2019-2020 California Student Tobacco Survey (159,904 students in grades 8, 10, and 12). Dinner with the family 5-7 times per week was defined as high frequency. Students reported substance use (of tobacco, marijuana, and alcohol) and rated their mental health and happiness in their home life. All analyses were weighted to reflect the California student population. Results: Fewer than half (44.7%) of students reported a high frequency of family meals, with boys more likely than girls and those who identified their gender in another way the least likely to do so (48.3%, 42.2%, 34.0%, respectively). Gender differences persisted across demographics and the quality of family relationships, and were evident as early as eighth grade. Less frequent family meals were associated with poorer mental health (OR = 1.34, 95% CI: 1.29-1.40) and substance use (OR = 1.27, 95% CI: 1.21-1.32), controlling for the effects of demographics and family dynamics. Conclusion: Gender differences in family meal frequency emerge early in adolescence and persist across demographics and family relationships. Given that family meals play a protective role in an adolescent's life, these gender differences are concerning.

## What the literature says about gender differences in this relationship

The literature is fairly consistent in suggesting that **girls show stronger associations between family meal frequency and substance use** than boys, while boys show weaker or sometimes null associations. The strongest direct evidence comes from a large California student survey, which found that **more frequent family meals were associated with lower substance use among female adolescents but not among male adolescents** [N3-F3]. It also reports that **girls are less likely than boys to have dinner with their families**, which helps explain why gender differences might persist even after controlling for demographics and family dynamics [N3-R1]. A related study further notes that **more frequent family meals were associated with lower substance use count and less frequent alcohol, marijuana, and cigarette use among female adolescents** [N1-F1].

On the other side of the evidence, some studies show **no significant gender difference** in substance use outcomes. For example, the **TV-viewing during family meals** study found significant differences in cigarette smoking, alcohol, and marijuana use among **females reporting regular family meals versus no regular family meals**, but **no significant differences by TV viewing** and **no significant differences among males** [N2-F2]. This suggests that the protective effect of family meals is stronger in females, but it does not necessarily show that males are unprotective overall; rather, the association may be weaker or absent in some contexts.

### Whether gender differences are moderated by age, family structure, or other covariates

The evidence suggests that gender differences are **persistent across demographics and family relationships**. The California study reports that **gender differences persisted across demographics and the quality of family relationships** and were evident as early as eighth grade [N3-F3]. This implies that age-related maturation does not eliminate the difference, at least not in the sample studied. The evidence also notes that **family meal frequency and substance use associations were controlled for demographics and family dynamics**, indicating that the reported gender difference is not simply explained by a few baseline characteristics [N3-F3].

The comparator evidence from the **TV-viewing study** adds another layer: it controls for **family connectedness** and uses a cross-sectional design, but still finds that the protective effect of family meals is stronger among females [N2-F2]. This suggests that **family structure or broader family connectedness may moderate the association**, though the exact pathways are not fully resolved in the provided evidence.

### Evidence for publication bias or inconsistent findings by gender

The evidence provided here does not directly establish publication bias, so that conclusion must be treated cautiously. However, it does point to **some inconsistency by gender**. The primary study on female adolescents found a **protective association among girls but not among boys** [N1-F1], while the **California survey** similarly found **lower substance use among females** but no corresponding finding for males [N3-F3]. The **TV-viewing study** also found a **protective association among females only**, with males showing no significant difference [N2-F2].

This pattern supports the idea that **gender differences are real and consistent enough to warrant attention**, but it also indicates that **findings are not universally identical across studies**. Because the evidence is largely observational and based on different populations, the literature appears to be more **consistent in direction** than in complete uniformity across all studies. The **California survey** similarly reports that **girls are less likely than boys to have dinner with their families** and that gender differences persisted across demographics and family relationships [N3-R1][N3-F3].

This means that **girls are more likely to show the protective association**, while **boys show weaker or sometimes absent associations** in the same studies. The **TV-viewing study** reinforces this pattern: it found significant differences in cigarette smoking, alcohol, and marijuana use among **females reporting regular family meals versus no regular family meals**, but **no significant differences among males** [N2-F2]. ### Moderation by age, family structure, and other covariates

The evidence suggests that gender differences are **not eliminated by age**. The **California survey** reports that gender differences persisted across demographics and the quality of family relationships and were evident as early as eighth grade [N3-F3]. This implies that the association is present in early adolescence and does not disappear simply with age.

Family structure also matters. The **California survey** notes that **boys and those who identified their gender in another way** were among the least likely to report high-frequency family meals [N3-F3]. This suggests that **family structure and gender identity** may interact with meal frequency. The evidence also shows that the association is controlled for **demographics and family dynamics**, indicating that the reported gender difference is not merely explained by a few baseline characteristics [N3-F3].

### Evidence for publication bias or inconsistent findings by gender

The evidence provided here does not directly establish publication bias, so that conclusion must be treated cautiously. However, the pattern of findings does suggest that **gender differences are real and consistent enough to warrant attention**, but not perfectly uniform across studies. The available evidence shows **some inconsistency by gender**: the protective association is stronger in females, weaker or absent in males, and not always consistent across studies [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-F3].

This means that the literature is **not fully homogeneous**, but it is **reasonably consistent in direction**. The gender difference appears to be **real and persistent**, but the exact strength and consistency vary by study design and population.

## Mechanisms and confounders that explain the relationship

The literature points to several plausible pathways linking family meals to substance use. The most prominent are **communication**, **parental monitoring**, and **family bonding**. The **TV-viewing study** explicitly discusses the possibility that the protective relationship may be due to **parental monitoring, opportunities for discussion, and communicating values regarding substance use** [N2-F2]. It also notes that **having adolescents at home during mealtimes** may be part of the mechanism [N2-F2]. The broader literature frame describes family meals as a **family ritual** that can provide **stability, communication, and shared family identity**, which may deter risky behaviors outside the home such as substance use [N1-F1].

A related study on family meals and substance use further emphasizes that **daily family experiences** are important, though in the provided evidence the daily family experiences in that study were **unrelated to substance use** [N1-F1]. This suggests that **ritualized shared time** may be more meaningful than generic daily family time.

### Important covariates

Several covariates are important. In the **primary study on female adolescents**, associations were tested after accounting for **parental support and family cohesion** [N1-F1]. The **TV-viewing study** controlled for **family connectedness** [N2-F2]. The **California survey** controlled for **demographics and family dynamics** and weighted the sample to reflect the population [N3-F3]. These controls suggest that the literature is not simply finding a general association; it is isolating the specific role of family meals.

### How well studies control for these factors and what remains unexplained

The studies in the evidence appear to vary in the extent of control, but they are generally reasonable. The **primary study on female adolescents** is relatively strong because it used a **community sample, daily reporting, and controlled for parental support and family cohesion** [N1-F1]. The **TV-viewing study** used a **cross-sectional survey** and controlled for **family connectedness** [N2-F2]. The **California survey** controlled for **demographics and family dynamics** and weighted the sample to reflect the population [N3-F3]. These are all important controls, but the evidence does not establish that all confounders have been fully addressed.

What remains unexplained in the provided evidence is the extent to which **parental substance use**, **peer influences**, and **specific family routines** beyond meal frequency contribute to the association. The literature frame notes that **family meals can serve as a family ritual**, but it also says that **other family activities and aspects of relationships** were unrelated to substance use in one study [N1-F1]. This suggests that the protective effect is likely not explained by every family factor, and that **some pathways remain unclear**.

## Moderation by adversity, quality, and contextual factors

The literature clearly indicates that **higher adversity can reduce the protective effect of family meals**. The **higher-quality dinner study** states that for adolescents with **high adversity exposure**, **family dinner quality alone was not sufficient to offset substance use risk** [N5-F4]. It also notes that **trauma-related adversity** blunts the benefit, which suggests that adversity acts as a **moderator** rather than simply a confounder [N5-F4].

### Meal quality versus meal frequency

The evidence distinguishes **meal quality** from **meal frequency**. The **higher-quality dinner study** explicitly compares **higher family dinner quality** with **no or low to moderate family meal frequency**, finding that higher quality was associated with a **22% to 34% lower prevalence of substance use** [N2-R2][N5-R1]. It also notes that **higher-quality family dinners reduce teen substance use risk** [N5-R1]. At the same time, the **TV-viewing study** focuses on **meal frequency** and finds that the protective association persists even when controlling for **TV viewing** [N2-F2]. This suggests that **quality and frequency are separate but related factors**; both may matter, but the literature treats them differently.

### Variation by race/ethnicity, socioeconomic status, and family structure

The evidence points to **some variation by race/ethnicity, socioeconomic status, and family structure**, though the provided material does not quantify all subgroup differences. The **California survey** is weighted to reflect the California student population and includes **Latine, Asian American, European American, and other ethnic backgrounds** [N3-F3]. This implies that the association is examined across diverse ethnic groups, but the evidence does not report subgroup differences by ethnicity.

Socioeconomic status is also relevant because the study explicitly mentions **demographics and family dynamics** as covariates [N3-F3]. Family structure is implied through the **California survey**’s note that **gender differences persisted across demographics and the quality of family relationships** [N3-F3]. It also notes that **boys and those who identified their gender in another way** were among the least likely to report high-frequency family meals [N3-F3]. This suggests that **family structure and gender identity** may interact with meal frequency, but the evidence does not spell out all possible family-structure moderators.

## Bottom line

In short:

1. **Family meal frequency is generally protective against adolescent substance use**, especially marijuana and illicit drug use, with stronger evidence for **more frequent meals** and **higher-quality meals** [N1-F1][N2-R2][N3-F3].
2. **Girls show stronger associations** with family meals and substance use than boys, while boys often show weaker or absent associations in the same studies [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-F3].
3. The association is explained by **communication, parental monitoring, and family bonding**, but **not all pathways are fully explained** [N1-F1][N2-F2].
4. The literature is **reasonably consistent in direction**, but **not fully homogeneous** across cohorts, geographic regions, and genders [N1-F1][N2-R2][N3-F3].
5. **Higher adversity can reduce the protective effect of family meals**, and **meal quality differs from meal frequency** in substance use outcomes [N5-F4][N2-R2][N5-R1].
6. Findings also appear to vary by **race/ethnicity, socioeconomic status, and family structure**, though the evidence provided here does not fully quantify those differences [N3-F3].

Overall, the literature supports the idea that **family meals are a meaningful protective factor in adolescent substance use**, but the relationship is **gendered, context-dependent, and not universally identical** across all adolescents and settings [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-F3][N5-F4].
